claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings is governed by the formation and mechanical integrity of an in-situ Cr-rich oxide tribofilm.
A nanocrystalline grain structure enhances the growth kinetics and cohesion of the Cr-rich oxide tribofilm.
The mechanically coherent oxide tribofilm reduces material removal under load.
The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has an average grain size of approximately 500 nm.
Increasing substrate bias and reducing deposition temperature can produce a FeNiCrCoCu coating with an average grain size below 50 nm.
Grain boundaries in the nanocrystalline coating provide rapid transport paths for Cr to the surface.
Rapid Cr supply produces a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 surface layer.
Nanocrystalline grains enhance short-circuit diffusion of Cr to the coating surface.
The resulting coherent oxide tribofilm carries the majority of the applied load.
The oxide tribofilm reduces direct metal-metal contact.
Nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have a steady-state wear rate 30–70% lower than approximately 500 nm-grain coatings tested under the same conditions.
Post-test analysis of the nanocrystalline coating will show a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 top layer.
The proposed mechanism applies in air from 500 to 800 °C, at normal loads of 1–10 N and sliding speeds around 10 mm/s.
Outside the stated temperature, load, and speed ranges, oxide kinetics or mechanical behavior may change.
Environmental humidity and minor variations in film chemistry may alter the magnitude of the wear-rate reduction.
Oxide-film continuity may depend on the sliding regime.
